fields.title: Where work is actually stuck
fields.keyTakeaway: Delivery speed is determined not by how fast code is written, but by how long a task waits between steps. Measure time from decision to user and see where it is spent.
fields.checkQuestion: Development takes 3 days, but the task ships in three weeks. Where to look for the difference?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **how to optimize value delivery flow?** In module R2, we planned a single delivery; here, how the delivery flow works and why it slows down.
fields.blocks/1/text: Running example: Polka is a fictional inventory app for small stores. The team grew from four people to eleven, and shipping became slower, not faster.
fields.blocks/2/title: Cycle time and where it gets lost
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Analyzed step by step, not by gut feeling
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Count from decision to user** — not from the start of development. Everything before is also time.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **Each step splits in two:** work and waiting. Waiting usually makes up most of it.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **Typical waiting points:** analytics queue, design waiting time, code review, QA queue, release window waiting time, sign-off approval.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **Work in progress** — how many tasks are active at once. The more tasks, the longer each one waits: this is arithmetic, not discipline.
fields.blocks/4/text: If the bottleneck is testing or sign-off queues, hiring a developer will add tasks to the queue and lengthen the wait. Before asking for headcount, measure where work sits idle.
fields.blocks/4/title: Hiring doesn't always speed things up
fields.blocks/5/text: Reducing cycle time is not an end in itself. Shipping unneeded features fast is worse than shipping necessary ones slowly; you fix flow when user feedback arrives later than subsequent decisions are made.
